title: Common peak dates force zero pairing excess; Arctic river tests show the limit of this timing control
abstract: We tested whether fixed peak dates identify a timing cause for excess summed river-flow peaks. We used 31 common certified years at Ob, Yenisey and Lena gauges in ArcticGRO v20261104, from 1980 to 2011. For the selected Yenisey-Lena pair, shifting each annual curve to its river-specific median seven-day peak date reduced the same-year excess over independent year pairing from 4,283 to -217 cubic metres per second. The contrast was 4,500, with conditional two-sided p = 0.0282. A flow-center shift gave a smaller, uncertain contrast of 1,639, with p = 0.3852. We prove that shifting both peaks to one common date makes every summed maximum equal to the sum of separate maxima. The pairing excess must then be zero for every data set. The audit confirmed this identity for all 2,883 river-year pair combinations. Thus loss of the excess after peak alignment does not by itself identify a shared timing cause. We also found that a prior pair study used four time groups in code but described three in text. The four-group calculation reproduces its published raw null mean. Short records, selected follow-up tests, year exchangeability, regulation, gauge error and absent coast travel times limit physical inference. Code, aggregate results, exact source hashes, uncertainty draws, audits and a figure are included. Source-level data remain external.

display.caption: Fixing peak dates nearly removes the pairing excess. This is limited evidence for a timing cause because exact common-date alignment forces zero excess. Intervals are conditional paired three-year block percentiles.

citations.reason: Prior summed peak association motivates a new timing-control test on overlapping data.
Prior pair results select the primary pair. We audit its text-to-code group discrepancy and test a new shift contrast.
